Surly

SUR-lee · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Surly is bad-tempered and unfriendly, often shown through a gruff, unwelcoming manner.

The surly bus driver never greeted a single passenger, just scowled and pulled away from the curb the second the doors closed.

Worked Example

Instead of the eager sales pitch customers expected, the surly clerk just muttered the price and looked back down at his phone.

Surly is mostly about a gruff, unwelcoming manner -- short answers, scowls, no eye contact -- rather than open arguing or shouting.

How Strong Is It? — short-tempered → surly → cantankerous

short-tempered vs. surly

short-tempered vs. surly: Being short-tempered is milder -- it just means quick to get annoyed, without necessarily showing the gruff unfriendliness that surly does.

cantankerous vs. surly

cantankerous vs. surly: Cantankerous (also in this unit) goes further than surly, adding active arguing and complaining on top of the gruff unfriendliness.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — sur-

root — sur-: a lord or master (a shifted spelling of sir; Middle English sirly, 'lordly')

suffix — -ly

suffix — -ly: having the quality of (Old English -lic)

Put it together

Put it together: Surly is built from sur- (a shifted spelling of sir, 'a lord or master') + -ly ('having the quality of') -- it originally meant 'lordly' or 'commanding,' describing someone who acted like a haughty master. Over time the spelling drifted from sirly to surly, and the meaning darkened into today's sense: gruff, unfriendly, and bad-tempered.

Use the root in a new word: sirrah

Use the root in a new word: sirrah: Sirrah was an old, often mocking way to address a man of lower rank -- built on the very same sir root that surly grew from, back when the word meant 'acting like a lord.'
